newsitem.title: KENYA: Protests broken up in Kenya, towns closed down.
newsitem.headline: Protests broken up in Kenya, towns closed down.

text.p: Riot police charged and fired tear gas to disperse demonstrators in Nairobi on Monday, sending hundreds of protesters running through the city centre stoning cars and buses.
"Moi must go. Moi must go," hundreds of opposition supporters chanted as they marched into the business centre of the city after dozens of police dispersed them from Uhuru Park.
President Daniel arap Moi says Monday's demonstrations, called across Kenya by opposition-backed groups demanding constitutional reforms, are illegal and aimed at inciting chaos.

Pro-reform groups said Monday would be the biggest day of political action at some 50 sites across the country to press for constitutional changes before presidential and parliamentary elections this year.
No date has been set for the polls.
Protesters stoned buses and cars on main highways in the city centre, running down streets pursued by groups of police and members of the paramilitary General Service Unit (GSU).
Police fired tear gas canisters and rubber bullets to disperse clusters of protesters outside the Serena hotel and beat protesters they caught, kicking and hitting them to the ground.
GSU and police fired tear gas inside All Saint's Cathedral and cornered several demonstrators in the pews and beat them. Three of the injured were later taken to hospital in cars.

"We were in the middle of the service when they broke in, fired tear gas into the house of God. This is Kenyan justice for you. Even in God's house they beat innocent protesters," said the Rev. Peter Njoka.
Except for the violent game of "cat and mouse" between demonstrators and the security forces, the centre of the city was deserted with all shops closed and many barricaded against looters.
The town of Nakuru, northwest of Nairobi, was also closed down as members of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union, wielding clubs, broke up demonstrations by hundreds of people.
Witnesses said at least two people were injured in Nakuru.
"We are telling our people don't fight," said Joseph Gichuru, local chairman of the opposition National Development Party. "For the place to be closed down, it is a success. The struggle must go on."
Police, wearing helmets and carrying shields, chased protesters across the nearby Uhuru Park in Nairobi, breaking up a meeting by opposition supporters who fled across the city.
On the northern outskirts of the capital, witnesses said students stopped vehicles and set them and tyres ablaze in the road and pelted passing cars and trucks with stones.
Many people stayed away from work to avoid the expected clashes between riot police and demonstrators in the city. Most schools were closed and asked parents to keep children at home.

State-run radio late on Sunday broadcast what it said was a statement from the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) -- which groups opposition parties, churches, human rights groups and other bodies -- saying Monday's rallies were cancelled.
But NCEC officials said the statement was bogus.
The NCEC last week called the rallies for July 7, a day in Kiswahili known as "Saba Saba" to commemorate a Nairobi rally seven years ago when at least 20 people were killed.
The NCEC said its supporters would be peaceful unless they were provoked. It argues the rallies are not illegal because they are "educational meetings" that do not need police licences.
The opposition wants review or repeal of six laws including the Public Order Act, seen as an instrument of suppression. It is also demanding greater access to state-controlled media.
Despite the opposition campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules and deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
